name: git pull
shortDescription: Fetch from a remote and integrate changes into the current branch. Essentially git fetch followed by git merge (or git rebase with --rebase).
detailedDescription:
The `git pull` command is a convenience that combines `git fetch` and `git merge` in a single step. It downloads new commits from the remote and immediately merges them into your current branch.

While convenient, `git pull` can surprise you with merge conflicts or unwanted merge commits. Many experienced developers prefer the two-step approach: `git fetch` first to see what's coming, then `git merge` or `git rebase` manually.

The `--rebase` flag is particularly important: instead of creating a merge commit, it replays your local commits on top of the remote changes. This keeps the history linear and clean — many teams require this via configuration.

parameters.description: Specify which remote and branch to pull from. If tracking is configured (via -u), you can just run `git pull` with no arguments.
After fetching, rebase the current branch on top of the upstream branch instead of merging. Creates a linear history without merge commits.
Explicitly use merge even if pull.rebase is configured globally.
Only proceed if the merge can be fast-forwarded. Refuses to create merge commits. Fails if local and remote have diverged.
Automatically stash local changes before pulling and re-apply them afterward. Saves you from having to manually stash.

examples.title: Basic pull from tracked upstream
examples.description: Pull the latest changes from the remote branch your local branch is tracking.
examples.code:
git pull

# If tracking isn't set up, specify explicitly:
git pull origin main

examples.title: Pull with rebase (clean history)
examples.description: Rebase local commits on top of remote changes instead of creating a merge commit.
examples.code:
git pull --rebase

# Make this the default for all repos:
git config --global pull.rebase true

examples.title: Pull with autostash
examples.description: When you have uncommitted changes but need to pull updates.
examples.code:
git pull --rebase --autostash

# Git automatically:
# 1. Stashes your changes
# 2. Pulls and rebases
# 3. Restores your stashed changes

examples.title: Safe pull (ff-only)
examples.description: Only pull if it's a simple fast-forward. This prevents accidental merge commits.
examples.code:
git pull --ff-only

# If local and remote have diverged, this fails with:
# fatal: Not possible to fast-forward, aborting.
# You can then decide to merge or rebase manually.

commonMistakes.text: `git pull` can create unexpected merge commits that clutter history. If you see 'Merge branch origin/main into main' commits, switch to `git pull --rebase` or use `git fetch` + manual merge.
Pulling with uncommitted changes can cause conflicts. Either commit your changes, stash them (`git stash`), or use `--autostash` to handle it automatically.
Set `git config --global pull.rebase true` to always rebase on pull. This is the most popular configuration among experienced Git users and prevents merge commit pollution.
The safest pull command is `git pull --rebase --autostash`. It handles dirty working directories, avoids merge commits, and keeps history clean.
